title: Two in the desert (Bava Metzia 62a)
hookLine: one flask, two travelers; Rabbi Akiva teaches that your own life comes first

lines: PUT ON YOUR OWN MASK FIRST.
cards: Every flight, the same speech: in case of a loss of cabin pressure, put on your own mask before helping others. To some ears it sounds almost selfish. Shouldn't you help the child first?
Then the logic lands: if you pass out, you can't help anyone. The Talmud has a much older, much harder version of that question. Two people are walking through the desert.
Only one of them has water, and there isn't enough for two. Two sages disagree about what to do.

teach.b: Here's the case, in tractate Bava Metzia. Two people are traveling, and one has a flask of water. If both drink, both will die.
If one drinks, he'll reach the next town alive. What should he do?
A sage named Ben Petura taught: better that both drink and both die, than that one watch the other die. Share it, whatever happens. A beautiful, brave answer.

teach.h: AKIVA: THAT HE MAY LIVE WITH THEE.
teach.b: Then Rabbi Akiva came and taught from a verse in Leviticus: "that thy brother may live with thee." With thee, Akiva said. Your brother lives alongside you.
So your own life comes first; the one with the flask may drink. The Talmud frames it this way: Ben Petura taught, until Rabbi Akiva came and taught otherwise.

This isn't a license for selfishness. The verse is about lending to someone in need without charging interest, about keeping your brother alive. And the case is an extreme one, where sharing means certain death for both.
Akiva isn't saying ignore other people. He's saying you're a person too. Your life counts in the math.
The airline card says something close, in a calmer voice: you can't care for anyone if you've collapsed.
Akiva's word is with: your life comes first, and your brother's lives alongside it.

how: Jewish ethics takes care of one's own health seriously, and Akiva's ruling, chayekha kodmin, your life comes first, is discussed in Jewish writing on triage and self-sacrifice.

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: both drink, even if both die

games.q: two of you in the desert. you have the only flask. if you share, both die. if you drink, you reach town. what does Rabbi Akiva say?
o: pour it out so no one has an unfair advantage.
games.why: Akiva read that thy brother may live with thee: your life comes first. Ben Petura had said both should drink.

practice: Ask where you're running low right now: sleep, food, quiet, time with friends, a doctor's appointment you keep putting off. Notice who depends on you, and that they depend on you being alive and well.
Then pick one small thing that would refill your flask, water, a walk, going to bed on time, and picture doing it not as a treat but as part of caring for them.

wordCard.voice: Rabbi Akiva, who taught that with one flask between two travelers in the desert, your life comes first, and your brother lives with you.

carryVoice: Your line: your life comes first. With them, not instead of them. Day two hundred eighty-five, done.
